GPUs

Received: 29 April 2025 / Accepted: 29 July 2026

Abstract
Feature selection is an important step in machine learning that can benefit from GPU
acceleration. As the number of GPU vendors increases, it is imperative to adapt
algorithms such as the minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) fea-
ture selection method to different backends that support several GPU architectures.
This work presents a multi-backend implementation of mRMR across CUDA, HIP, and
SYCL, and studies its performance when combined with Bayesian optimization and
transfer learning to automatically tune execution parameters for different platforms
and datasets. Our experimental results show that when tuned, CUDA and HIP achieve
comparable performance on NVIDIA architectures, while SYCL exhibits a moder-
ate performance gap. Overall, this work highlights the impact of backend choice and
autotuning on GPU-accelerated feature selection and provides insights into deploying
mRMR across heterogeneous environments.

Keywords GPU · Feature selection · mRMR · CUDA · HIP · SYCL

1 Introduction

In recent years, the demand for efficient high-performance computing (HPC) has
surged due to the increasing use of data-intensive applications. Among the various
HPC architectures, GPUs can effectively deliver impressive performance for massively
parallel problems and have become increasingly powerful with relatively low power
consumption. Machine learning (ML) and data analysis workflows are among the
most computationally demanding fields today, and many algorithms leverage GPUs to
accelerate their execution. For example, feature selection (FS) [1], a key preprocessing
technique in many classical ML and data analysis pipelines used to reduce dataset
dimensionality, is a good candidate for GPU acceleration due to its high computational
intensity, involving highly demanding calculations on large datasets.
    Among the various methods for FS [2], one of the most popular is the minimum
Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) [3], which balances high relevance with
low redundancy. In practice, mRMR has been applied across diverse domains, includ-
ing large-scale marketing and personalization systems, industrial process monitoring,
and hyperspectral image analysis, where reducing redundancy and dimensionality is
critical for both performance and interpretability [4, 5]. Although there is an earlier
version of mRMR that can take advantage of GPU hardware [6], it was designed only
for NVIDIA’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA1 ) framework. CUDA
is the default choice for developers targeting NVIDIA GPUs [7] due to its maturity,
extensive library support, and optimizations for NVIDIA hardware, but its usability
is limited because it cannot run on alternative hardware platforms.
    To address the need for cross-platform GPU programming, AMD developed the
Heterogeneous-Compute Interface for Portability (HIP2 ), a framework designed to
enable code portability across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. They have also developed
HIPify,3 a tool that automatically adapts CUDA source code to HIP, extending its
applicability to more hardware platforms. HIP has become more attractive due to
AMD’s increasing market share in the HPC sector and the growing demand for a
CUDA alternative that is compatible with AMD’s ROCm4 ecosystem. Despite its
potential, the HIP ecosystem is still maturing and performance on non-AMD GPUs
can vary, making it a critical focus when comparing GPU frameworks.
    In addition, the Khronos Group introduced SYCL,5 a single-source, C++-based
framework that aims to unify the programming experience for heterogeneous comput-
ing by supporting a wide range of processors, including GPUs, CPUs, and FPGAs. As
an open standard, SYCL is designed to support multiple vendors and architectures,
providing a high degree of portability. With recent advances, such as the development
of oneAPI’s Data Parallel C++ (DPC++), SYCL has gained relevance in the HPC
and ML communities for workloads that require flexibility across different hardware

environments [8]. However, the performance of SYCL in computationally demanding
applications such as FS remains relatively underexplored.
   The main goal of this work is to develop multiple backend implementations of
mRMR that extend the usability of this FS method across different GPU architectures.
The novel implementations include optimizations tailored to CUDA, HIP, and SYCL,
achieving high performance across different hardware platforms. In our work, we
combine Bayesian Optimization (BO) and Transfer Learning (TL) for selecting the
best configuration parameters (adapted to the dataset, problem size, and characteristics
of the underlying hardware).
   Performance portability has been defined in different ways in the literature, often
requiring a single implementation to achieve near-peak performance across multi-
ple architectures. In practice, however, achieving such behavior is challenging due to
architectural differences and backend-specific optimizations. In this work, we adopt
a pragmatic view of performance portability, focusing on the ability to obtain high
performance across platforms with limited tuning effort. This reflects real-world sce-
narios in which autotuning and backend specialization are commonly used to bridge
performance gaps between architectures.
   In summary, these are the main contributions of this work:


 • Novel versions of the mRMR FS method using HIP and SYCL that can run on
   non-NVIDIA GPUs, highlighting the implementation particularities of each pro-
   gramming model. They are open source and publicly available6 so that the scientific
   community can use them to accelerate their analyses. We also release further opti-
   mizations over our previous CUDA implementation for the mRMR algorithm [6].
 • An autotuning study based on BO and TL to efficiently identify high-performance
   configurations across datasets, backends, and platforms.
 • A performance comparison for equivalent CUDA, HIP, and SYCL mRMR
   implementations on different NVIDIA GPU architectures, providing insight into
   selecting the optimal programming model for GPU-based FS tasks.
 • An exploratory cross-platform evaluation of the HIP backend, illustrating how the
   same implementation behaves across different GPU architectures under a fixed
   experimental setup.


   The remainder of the manuscript is organized as follows: Sect. 2 reviews previ-
ous research on GPU-accelerated FS methods, as well as on comparative analyses of
CUDA, HIP, and SYCL. Section 3 provides an overview of key concepts, includ-
ing FS and cross-platform GPU compatibility. The implementation details and
framework-specific optimizations for GPU-based mRMR are described in Sect. 4. The
experimental results evaluating the performance of the implementations in the setup
described in Sect. 5 with the performance portability search detailed in Sect. 6 are pre-
sented in Sect. 7. Finally, Sect. 8 summarizes the findings and highlights avenues for
future research.

2 Related work

As previously mentioned, mRMR has already been parallelized for NVIDIA GPUs
using CUDA [6] and is publicly available (along with other FS methods) as part of
the Parallel-FST library.7 Although there have been previous efforts to exploit GPUs
to accelerate other FS methods (e.g., [9–11]), none of them are based on either HIP
or SYCL for cross-platform execution. This makes our study of great interest to the
scientific community.
   Regarding performance comparisons between CUDA, HIP, and SYCL, several
works have tested their performance using a variety of workloads and applications
on different types of GPUs. Many authors have focused on bioinformatics applica-
tions due to their high computational cost, which makes GPUs a good choice for
accelerating their analyses. One example is ADEPT [12], a tool for DNA and protein
sequence alignment. This tool was originally developed in CUDA and designed for
NVIDIA GPUs, but was later translated to HIP and SYCL to evaluate its portability
[13]. The translation to SYCL proved to be significantly more challenging than the
translation to HIP. In terms of performance, the HIP version matches the speed of
the CUDA version, while the SYCL implementation is about twice as slow. Another
recent study focused on an open-source bioinformatics kernel for all-pairs distance
calculation [14], which implements GPU kernels optimized for memory accesses,
reduced memory footprints, and effective use of the memory hierarchy on NVIDIA
and AMD GPUs. The authors analyzed the GPU instructions generated by the com-
pilers to understand the code optimizations and performance gaps. They concluded
that CUDA and HIP kernels outperform SYCL kernels due to factors such as memory
address sizes, memory access widths, and sub-word accesses.
   A more recent paper [15] completed a very interesting study of NVIDIA, Intel,
and AMD GPUs on exascale supercomputers. Their workload performs a massively
parallel blood flow (hemodynamic) simulation based on the lattice Boltzmann method
for fluid dynamics. The authors found that the three programming models achieved
high performance on these GPUs. However, SYCL development required more effort
to implement efficient code, while an almost direct translation from CUDA to HIP
was sufficient to achieve high performance. Other works have compared CUDA with
SYCL only [16, 17], excluding HIP from the analysis.
   Although comparing the performance of CUDA, HIP, and SYCL on complete
applications is interesting for the HPC community, the conclusions may be closely
tied to a specific domain. Another approach is to focus on common kernels or specific
functions that are present in different types of applications. An example is the test
suite in [18], which uses tensor contractions for high-dimensional general matrix
multiplications. Specifically, they compare the original CUDA version generated by
COGENT [19], a CUDA generator for tensor contractions, with automatic translations
to HIP and SYCL on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, highlighting that CUDA and HIP
outperform SYCL. The authors identified occupancy and data movement resulting
from the use of local memory as the primary factors contributing to this performance
difference. In addition, another work [20] focused on stencil computations, which are

   While CUDA, HIP, and SYCL require tuning for optimized performance, the best
tuning values depend on the programming model, execution model, and compiler effi-

tuning approaches, BO-based autotuning has become popular for HPC tuning [22–26],
modeling the performance objective function as a probabilistic surrogate and leading
to optimal parameter selection with minimal configuration evaluations. This black-box
approach is very well suited for tuning complex systems where performance is influ-
enced by multiple interdependent parameters and hardware-specific features, such as
CUDA, HIP, and SYCL applications running on different platforms. Specifically, we
use our multi-platform tuning tool DFTuning [27] to perform the complex autotuning
search of this work. This tool uses GPTune [28] as its underlying BO engine to optimize
the execution across different datasets, backends, and hardware platforms by sharing
tuning information (through TL) for a predefined set of performance parameters.
   Our work contributes to the scientific community by providing a multi-backend
implementation of mRMR, which can leverage multiple HPC hardware platforms
thanks to state-of-the-art autotuners. In addition, to the best of our knowledge, this
study presents the first performance analysis of CUDA, HIP, and SYCL for a FS
algorithm.


3 Background

This section describes several concepts that will be necessary to understand the imple-
mentations developed as part of this work.

3.1 Feature selection

FS is a technique that finds the best subset of features for a given dataset. Depending on
the data analysis step in which FS is applied, we can identify three different approaches:
 • Filters, where FS is applied as an independent step before training an ML model.
   The dimensionality of the dataset is reduced with FS so that the training step runs
   faster.
 • Wrapper approaches, where the FS and the ML model are tightly coupled. The
   subset of selected features is built iteratively, using the model to evaluate its good-
   ness.
 • Embedded approaches that apply FS as an inherent part of the model construction.
   For example, FS can decide which feature to use as a splitting condition at a given
   node when building a decision tree.
   The mRMR algorithm is an FS filter that uses Mutual Information (MI) to measure
the relevance of a feature.

3.2 Cross-platform GPU compatibility and autotuning

GPU vendors such as NVIDIA and AMD provide low-level programming models like
CUDA or AMD ROCm that deliver high performance by interacting closely with the
hardware. However, this comes at a cost, as code written for one platform is not easily

portable to another. To address this, some higher-level programming models support
cross-platform compatibility. For example, programs written in OpenCL9 can take
advantage of parallelism in GPUs and even in multicore CPUs. Built on the principles
of OpenCL, but with a more modern API, SYCL targets GPUs from different vendors,
CPUs, and even FPGAs, using a single-source codebase. Another example is HIP,
which can be compiled for both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.
    Therefore, to target multiple platforms, we can either rely on having multiple back-
ends or use a higher-level programming model that supports a wide range of platforms.
The balance between performance and portability, known as performance portability,
ensures that applications can achieve high performance on multiple hardware plat-
forms.
    Performance is determined by a set of parameters known as performance param-
eters. By expressing the code in terms of these parameters and assigning different
values to them, we can gain control over the performance of the application. The auto-
matic process of finding optimal values for these parameters is known as autotuning,
which allows applications to achieve near-optimal performance across a wide range
of platforms without extensive manual effort, making it an important component of
modern HPC.
    However, identifying the optimal values for these parameters is challenging in
the exascale era due to the increasing complexity and heterogeneity of systems. The
large number of performance parameters (application-, framework-, and architecture-
dependent) makes exhaustive search methods unfeasible, since they require evaluating
every possible configuration. Instead, ML-based approaches, in particular BO [30],
provide a better alternative to address this challenge. BO treats performance optimiza-
tion as a black-box optimization problem, which enables the discovery of near-optimal
parameter configurations while significantly reducing the search cost. BO solves the
tuning process as an iterative optimization problem where the objective is to iden-
tify optimal parameters with minimal evaluations. It uses a surrogate model, often a
Gaussian process, to approximate the application’s performance (objective function)
based on performance configurations (parameters). The surrogate model predicts both
the mean and the uncertainty (variance) of performance for new configurations. This
predictive approach allows BO to strategically explore the parameter space while
balancing exploration and exploitation in a trade-off fashion:
  • Exploration focuses on less known regions of the search space to gain new infor-
     mation.
  • Exploitation focuses on refining high-performing regions already identified.
    The acquisition function guides this trade-off by assigning a score to each configura-
tion to prioritize either exploration or exploitation. As new data are introduced through
evaluations, the surrogate model is constantly retrained and progressively improving
its accuracy to guide the search. Unlike grid search or random search, which may
require a larger number of evaluations to explore the large search space, BO builds an
accurate surrogate model with fewer function evaluations [23, 24, 28].
    While traditional BO-based autotuning operates as a black-box framework within a
fixed platform, performance portability poses additional challenges when applications

   In our study, we use DFTuning [27], which builds upon the GPTune framework

multitask approach enables the use of TL. By transferring knowledge from previ-

to minimize redundant search exploration and thus promote performance portability,
making it particularly well suited for tuning mRMR on different GPU architectures.


4 GPU implementation of the mRMR algorithm

The GPU implementation of mRMR developed in this work builds on the caching-
based version presented in Algorithm 2 of Sect. 3.1.2, which introduces several key
modifications to increase performance over any previous implementation [6]. It adopts
a resident-dataset approach in which the dataset is transferred to GPU memory only
once and remains on the device for the entire FS process, while the host orchestrates the
computation by managing batching, memory management, and kernel launches. To
ensure portability, our work implements the GPU-based mRMR algorithm across three
different backends (CUDA, HIP, and SYCL) to target different hardware platforms.
These backends expose a number of performance parameters that need to be tuned.
To achieve performance portability, Sect. 6 explains how to use DFTuning to find the
optimal values for these parameters for each backend, dataset, and hardware platform.

4.1 Modifications to the mRMR algorithm

Although the joint probability in Eq. 1, p(x, y), depends on the features involved, the
marginal probabilities, p(x) and p(y), remain constant for each feature. Therefore,
they can be computed only once and cached for later use. Compared to previous imple-
mentations, we now cache both marginal probabilities and simplify their computation
by keeping them resident in GPU global memory for different kernel executions. A
high-level diagram of the modified mRMR is shown in Fig. 2. By precomputing all
marginal probabilities and using global memory, we save GPU cycles and reduce
reliance on shared memory, which enhances the occupancy of GPU kernels. Note that
in our implementation, the marginal probabilities are computed on the GPU, even
though the runtime of this step is almost negligible (and therefore it is not highlighted
in Fig. 2).

   With the modifications introduced so far, the computation of the MI consists of two
steps: (1) calculate the joint frequencies; (2) calculate the MI using the marginal and
joint frequencies and converting them to probabilities. These two steps are performed
within a single GPU kernel, using one thread block per feature, i.e., given a fixed
feature Y , every thread block is responsible for computing the MI between a feature in
the dataset and Y . Threads within each block work together on different samples. The
amount of memory required for the structure may differ between pairs of features, since
their alphabets may be different. Following the approach of previous implementations,
we developed a custom memory management system based on pools of GPU global
memory managed by the CPU. In addition, we divided the workload into batches,
with each kernel invocation computing the MI for a subset of features. This design is
motivated primarily by memory constraints. Since the dataset and one joint-frequency
structure per processed feature must reside in GPU memory, processing all features in
a single kernel invocation may exceed the available memory for datasets with a large
number of features. Batching allows us to bound memory usage while avoiding the
high overhead of launching one kernel per feature.

   This design also enables the overlap of host-side preparation and device execution
using asynchronous streams, as illustrated in Fig. 3. In particular, the host iterates
over batches, performing memory allocation, data transfers, and initialization for each
batch, while previously submitted batches are executed on the GPU. A similar strategy
was used in the original CUDA implementation of mRMR [6] and is adapted here to
the multi-backend setting.
   Theoretically, it is possible to use an arbitrarily large number of streams in some
devices, which would eliminate synchronizations by assigning a unique stream per
batch. However, this approach is not feasible because a maximum number of streams
must be set beforehand in order to perform memory allocations. Note that the allo-
cated memory grows not only with the batch size but also with the maximum number
of streams, which can significantly impact performance. Therefore, a bounded num-
ber of streams is used and reused in a cyclic manner across batches. Consequently,
before submitting a new batch to a stream that has already been used, the host must
synchronize that stream to ensure that all previously enqueued operations have com-
pleted. These synchronizations are thus required to guarantee correctness when reusing
streams, rather than due to data dependencies between batches. The optimal number
of streams used may vary from dataset to dataset. Therefore, it has been exposed as a
performance parameter to be tuned in our implementation.

    Although previous implementations used 16-bit precision for both marginal and
joint frequencies, this work employs 16-bit precision only for joint frequencies and 32-
bit for marginal frequencies. By moving marginal frequencies out of shared memory,
we increase the capacity to store joint frequencies in shared memory. However, from
a performance perspective, there is an inflection point where the reduced occupancy
caused by using shared memory does not offset the increased latency of accessing
global memory. To address this, this work also considers the maximum shared mem-
ory usage per thread block as a performance parameter. If the data structure does not fit
in the specified amount of shared memory, then global memory is selected specifically
for that feature. This performance parameter allows to establish a balance between:
(1) maximizing the likelihood that shared memory is used for the joint frequencies,
and (2) maximizing the number of active thread blocks on the GPU (related to occu-
pancy). Section 4.2 explains some characteristics that each platform and programming
model natively exposes, which can improve GPU performance and were considered
as performance parameters in our work.

4.2 Backends for performance portability

Our GPU strategy, described in Sect. 4.1, can be adapted to different program-
ming models. Adaptation to each model requires adhering to implementation-specific
details, including variations in naming conventions (e.g., the concept of “streams” in
CUDA and HIP is equivalent to “queues” in SYCL). This work adopts the CUDA
terminology, as it is the most widely recognized standard in the HPC community.
   Although CUDA, HIP, and SYCL provide different APIs for GPU control, they
share several core functionalities, such as kernel execution, memory management,
and asynchronous task handling. CUDA and HIP provide similar mechanisms for
these functionalities, while SYCL often takes a different approach. The following
examples from our mRMR implementation illustrate key differences and necessary
adjustments in the codebase:
 • Writing and compiling kernels While CUDA and HIP define a kernel as a C-style
   function, SYCL provides a higher-level approach that allows kernels to be defined
   as named function objects or lambda functions.
 • Starting kernel executions CUDA and HIP support a common syntax kernel«<
   gridDim, blkDim, shMem, stream»>(args...) to configure the grid
   dimension, block dimension, shared memory per block, and id of the stream for
   which the kernel is launched. This call acts as a wrapper to the cudaLaunchKernel
   and hipLaunchKernelGGL functions, respectively. SYCL follows an object-
   oriented syntax. Instead of having grid and block dimensions, SYCL specifies the
   partitioning of the workload by a global range (total number of threads) and a local
   range (number of threads per block). In all three frameworks, kernel launches are
   asynchronous to the host, meaning that kernels are scheduled for execution on the
   GPU and control is returned to the CPU.

 • Managing memory CUDA and HIP provide functions for allocating and deallo-
   cating buffers on global memory with different characteristics (e.g., non-pageable
   memory), specific memory layouts (e.g., padded), and support for asynchronous
   operations. Shared memory can be allocated statically, if the size is known at com-
   pile time, by specifying it in the kernel. If the size is known at runtime, it must be
   specified when launching the kernel. Instead, SYCL exposes two mechanisms for
   dealing with memory management:
      – The Buffer-Accessor (BA) model provides a high-level abstraction of the mem-
        ory. Buffers are an abstraction for a view of the memory, accessible by the host
        or the device, and accessors are the abstractions used to read or write memory
        from a buffer.
      – The Unified Shared Memory (USM) is the lower-level option because it relies
        on pointers and various functions to allocate different types of memory.
   The USM approach was used in this work to keep more control over global-
   memory operations and because the resulting code structure is similar to that of
   CUDA and HIP. However, the shared memory must be handled in a BA fashion.
   To set memory, the {cuda,hip}Memset functions are used in CUDA and HIP,
   while the fill method of the Queue class is used in SYCL.
 • Managing asynchronous streams The main difference in handling streams is that
   CUDA and HIP have an implicit stream where tasks are enqueued by default. If
   more streams are needed, they must be created and destroyed using the appropriate
   functions. Instead, there are no default streams in SYCL, and at least one queue
   must be explicitly created to submit any work to the GPU. In addition, more queues
   can be created to take advantage of inter-stream asynchrony.
 • Identifying the active thread and block In our approach, mRMR uses the thread
   block index to identify the feature being processed, while the thread index is used to
   calculate the memory addresses accessed by each thread. In CUDA and HIP, these
   indices (as well as the dimensions of the grid and the thread blocks) are obtained
   within the kernel from specific built-in variables. This is different in SYCL, where
   an object is mapped to each unit of parallel execution, such as a work-item, and
   indices and dimensions are obtained using get_* methods.
 • Addressing atomic operations Atomic operations are executed in the MI compu-
   tation to accumulate the data frequencies as well as the partial MI of each thread.
   In CUDA and HIP, there are specific functions used for this purpose. In SYCL,
   atomics require some more work to set them up. First, an atomic reference must
   be constructed for a given memory address, and then a fetch method is used to
   increment the value.

   Some constraints are enforced directly in the mRMR code to prevent performance
losses due to inefficient configurations. However, they must also be defined in DFTun-
ing to avoid wasting resources evaluating ineffective regions of the search space.
   In addition, we can leverage the knowledge from previous searches to guide new
searches (i.e., for different input parameters) by focusing only on already discovered
high-performance regions of a similar search space. This is achievable by TL, which
effectively reduces the number of executions BO needs to find near-optimal configu-
rations. For example, in a new tuning search where the only difference is the selected
dataset, some good values of the performance parameters are likely to remain similar
across datasets. BO can take advantage of this prior information to reduce the number
of evaluations needed. A key innovation introduced in [27] is the use of TL to incor-
porate search knowledge from previous platforms into new ones, thereby improving
portability optimization.
   DFTuning builds the initial surrogate model by evaluating some random con-
figurations. Then, new configurations are interactively evaluated following the
exploration/exploitation paradigm until the stopping criterion is met. Specifically,
DFTuning was configured with a stopping criterion based on a window size of the
last W = 20 executions and a threshold of τ = 1.5%. If no configuration improves
the previous runtime by at least τ within W executions, the search is terminated.
To reduce noise in the measurements, each configuration was run five times and the
average was calculated.
   The tuning experiments were conducted with k = 20 selected features to keep the
search cost manageable. In our GPU implementation of mRMR, the configurable per-
formance parameters affect the computation of feature scores, which is the device-side
step repeated at each selection iteration. These parameters do not alter the algorithmic
structure for different values of k; therefore, increasing k primarily results in addi-

7.3 Cross-platform behavior of HIP

Table 8 shows the runtimes achieved by the best configuration found for each dataset
on each platform using the HIP implementation. The table also includes the speedup
of each platform relative to Frontier, which is the slowest platform in our results. As
noted above, Frontier did not have full SYCL support at the time of this work.
    These results provide an exploratory view of how the same HIP implementation
behaves across different execution environments. We emphasize that these platforms
differ substantially in architecture, memory hierarchy, clock frequency, and software
stack, and that the MI250X GPU is evaluated using a single die. Therefore, the results
presented in this section should not be interpreted as a controlled comparison across
GPU vendors, but rather as observations specific to the considered implementations
and experimental setup.
    Under these conditions, we observe that the Lovelace system achieves an average
speedup of 1.47x and 2.22x over Perlmutter and Frontier, respectively, while Perl-
mutter achieves an average speedup of 1.48x over Frontier. For MNIST, the smallest
dataset, the differences are more pronounced. This can be attributed to fixed overheads
(such as data transfers, CPU-side FS, and kernel launch costs) having a relatively larger
impact when the computational workload is small.
    The observed performance differences across systems are influenced by multiple
interacting factors related to both hardware characteristics and software execution.
In particular, the mRMR workload relies heavily on atomic operations with irregular
memory access patterns during frequency computation, followed by a more structured
but computationally intensive MI calculation. The first step has been empirically iden-
tified as the dominant bottleneck due to its reliance on global-memory atomics and
limited locality, while the second step benefits from more regular access patterns.
Several architectural factors may contribute to the observed behavior, including dif-
ferences in atomic operation latency, cache hierarchy (especially L2 cache capacity
and behavior), register usage and its impact on occupancy, and operating frequency.
For example, global-memory atomics are coordinated across thread blocks and may
rely on different memory subsystems depending on the architecture. Larger L2 caches

7.4 Discussion

Regarding performance, the experimental results from the previous subsection do not
show a significant difference between the runtimes of the HIP and CUDA imple-
mentations. Although there is a high variance depending on the characteristics of the
analyzed dataset, the SYCL implementation shows an average performance loss of
about 6% (see Sect. 7.2). This validates our decision to implement a multi-backend
approach rather than adopting SYCL (the most portable of the three programming
models as of today). The observed SYCL behavior is in line with the conclusions of
previous works [13, 18] already cited in Sect. 2. In our case, the performance drop
may be related to overheads in certain operations (such as kernel invocation and data
transfer to the GPU), compiler/runtime behavior, and the lack of an equivalent to the
__launch_bounds__ qualifier at the time of this research.
   These results should be interpreted in the context of the software environments
reported in Table 3. Since this work compares backend implementations compiled
with different toolchains and runtimes, the observed differences reflect the combined
effect of the programming model, compiler/runtime maturity, and system configura-
tion. In particular, the small differences observed between CUDA and HIP on NVIDIA
GPUs should be interpreted as comparable performance rather than as a meaningful
advantage of either backend.
   Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of BO-based searches com-
pared to random searches [23, 24, 28], as well as search acceleration when using TL
from previous searches in similar architectures [27]. In our results, the BO-guided step
that follows the random evaluation achieved 22% faster configurations. For example,
compared to the HIP implementation, SYCL shows an average performance drop
of 9.33% when running random configurations, while this drop is reduced to about
6.16% when using the guided search. The search space for each backend, platform, and
dataset consists of more than 100 million combinations in total, while the BO-based
search finishes after an average of 49 evaluations. While we recognize that these BO
searches may not have explored the optimal configuration during these evaluations, as

    Furthermore, as shown in Sect. 7.3, performance differences are observed across the
evaluated systems when using the same HIP implementation. Under the experimental
conditions considered in this work, the AMD MI250X exhibits lower performance
than the NVIDIA A100. These results depend on multiple factors, including the char-
acteristics of the mRMR workload (which relies heavily on atomic operations), the
implementation strategy, the HIP backend, the compiler and runtime environment, and
the use of a single die of the MI250X. Several factors may contribute to this behavior.
In particular, since the implementation is latency-bound due to the use of atomics,
it is relevant to consider how atomic operations are handled on different platforms.
While we use INT32 atomics to compute frequencies, some architectures may require
specific compiler options (e.g., -munsafe-fp-atomics) to fully exploit hardware
capabilities, and not using them may result in missed optimization opportunities12 .13
    While tools exist to quantify portability effort [33], such an analysis is beyond the
scope of this work. However, our experience as developers provides valuable insights.
Translating CUDA code to HIP was straightforward, given the similar C-based syn-
tax and programming structure. Perhaps the most significant difference is that some
recent CUDA features may not yet be available or mature in HIP. Porting the imple-
mentation to SYCL required more substantial restructuring. The underlying GPU
execution hierarchy is conceptually similar, but SYCL exposes it through different
abstractions. These differences made the SYCL implementation less direct and intro-
duced a steeper learning curve, while also providing flexibility to target both GPUs
and multicore CPUs.
    Finally, we note that this study focuses on the mRMR algorithm, which is rep-
resentative of MI-based FS methods. Its implementation is dominated by histogram
construction, atomic operations, and irregular memory accesses, which are also present
in other MI- and Conditional MI (CMI)-based methods. While different algorithms
may combine these operations in different ways, potentially affecting portability and
tuning behavior, we expect that several of the observed trends extend to this broader
class of methods. Therefore, the conclusions of this work should be interpreted within
the scope of MI-based FS. In this context, and considering our mRMR implementation
and the tested platforms, our observations suggest the following guidelines:

 • For porting an existing CUDA mRMR codebase to AMD GPUs, HIP is a natural
   choice, as it requires limited restructuring and enables execution on the tested
   AMD platform.
 • For this workload on NVIDIA GPUs, CUDA and HIP achieve comparable opti-
   mized performance, making HIP a reasonable option when a CUDA-like codebase
   targeting both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs is desired.
 • SYCL requires more substantial restructuring and is slower in our NVIDIA exper-
   iments, but remains attractive when broader source-level portability is the main
   objective.

8 Conclusions

We have studied the implementation of GPU-accelerated FS using the mRMR algo-
rithm across multiple programming backends (CUDA, HIP, and SYCL), analyzing
how autotuning techniques can be used to obtain efficient configurations across differ-
ent execution environments. In this work, we formulated the optimization process as
a search problem and applied BO with TL to tune the performance parameters of each
backend–platform combination. On average, the search required only 49 evaluations
per scenario, representing a small fraction of the total search space.
    The performance evaluation showed that when properly tuned, CUDA and HIP
achieve comparable performance on NVIDIA platforms. This indicates that HIP can
effectively exploit the underlying hardware while maintaining a CUDA-like program-
ming model, making it a practical option when targeting multiple platforms with
similar codebases. In contrast, SYCL exhibited a moderate performance gap in our
experiments on NVIDIA GPUs, which may be related to differences in runtime behav-
ior, compiler maturity, and the lack of certain low-level optimization mechanisms
available in CUDA and HIP at the time of this study. The results also illustrate the
importance of autotuning in adapting performance parameters to each backend and
execution environment. The use of BO enabled the efficient exploration of a large con-
figuration space and consistently identified high-performance configurations without
requiring exhaustive searches.
